title: Refused service in Kankakee and other Illinois incidents
summary: In 1930 he and banjoist Mike McKendrick were refused lunch at a bus stop in Kankakee, and a cook came out with a cleaver. With the Virginia Ravens they could play dances but not eat or sleep in some Illinois towns.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: But, you know, obviously in traveling around all those years in, you know, with the bands you ran into this all the time.
Oh, well, you know, I know what to

expect because in the year earlier we had eaten in a -- many a kitchen, back up in a restaurant and also taken food out, and in fact, one time we was coming with Bernie Young's band and had gone down to Tulsa, Oklahoma. We -- some of the guys came back in cars, and Mike McKendrick -- I don't know if you remember him, the banjo player, used to be with Louis -- he and I came back on the bus, on the Greyhound bus.

And we were having a ball on the bus. I had my horn, and I'm playing, and Mike, he had his banjo, and the people were singing and everything. So finally we pulled into Kankokee, Illinois, to the bus stop for lunch or something. So everybody gets out and goes in to eat. Mike and I get on out and go in and sit down, sat there for about ten, 15 minutes, and nobody waited on us.
So finally the waitress came over and said, 'we can't serve colored people in here,' you know.
This was Illinois?
Yeah. So I said -- well, this is 1930, you see -- so I said, 'well, can we get some sandwich or something to go out?' And she says, 'okay, we'll fix you something to go out.'

Well, in the meantime Mike got mad. He goes out, and he -- he had a, was carrying a .45 pistol on him, you know, and he went out to get a policeman to find out whether we could. Anyway, while he was gone, the cook came running out of the
kitchen with a cleaver.
This is a white cook?
Yeah, he comes running out of the kitchen with a cleaver.
At you?

And -- but the waitress stopped him, you know, he come out, says, 'Didn't you tell those black so and so's that they couldn't eat in here?' And she says, 'well, they are going to take it out.' Well, I just got up. I was getting ready to let them have the stool.

And then when Mike got back, she had calmed him, and he went back in the kitchen. So I said -- I told Mike, let's go. We didn't even wait for the sandwiches, just went on out and got in the car. But he was going to --
If Mike had been there when --
If Mike had been there, Mike would have shot him, and we would have both been at Joliet, some place up there.
(Laughter.)
No, you ran into a lot of things on the road.
I remember in another town in Illinois with the Virginia Ravens we couldn't -- we couldn't eat there, or we couldn't sleep there, but we could play the dance.
We'd get in there, say, like at 8:00 and play the dance, start the dance at 8:30, and soon as it was over, we'd
leave and go somewhere else. Illinois was pretty rough in those days. In fact, The Loop in Chicago was bad news for -- you couldn't even go downtown and eat.
